slides.title: Choosing a microcontroller
slides.presenterNote: Her 17x slide 22. The block was modernized at her request (2026-09-13): Nucleo-anchored instead of Arduino-anchored, current market, and a how-to-choose method for a student picking a part for a project in another course. Still instructor-only until she says otherwise. If run, it is realistically ≈ 10–12 min, and the minutes come out of the 70-minute demo block (the slack is only 2).

slides.title: Start with what your project needs
slides.body: In another course you may have to pick a microcontroller for a project. Start by working out what the project needs:
items: Which peripherals does the project need, and how many of each: ADC channels, PWM timers, UART, I2C, SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface), USB? We used most of these this term.
Does the project need WiFi or Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)? Each requires a part with that radio built in, so answer this first: it rules out most of the catalog.
If it runs on a battery, the sleep-mode current matters as much as the feature list.
How much flash and RAM, and how many pins? Count your signals and round up.
Then pick a part whose ecosystem you can use, and prototype on a development board rather than on a bare chip.
For example, a scale that reads a load cell and shows grams needs two ADC channels, one I2C display, no wireless, and wall power. That list is what you type into a search filter.
slides.presenterNote: New slide (her ask, 2026-09-13: students are often lost choosing a part for another class's project). The method: requirements first, ecosystem second, chip last. The peripherals line is the payoff of the whole term: they can read a part's peripheral list now and know what every entry means. If run live, ask the room to name the peripherals their own final project used — it is the same list-making move, and everyone can answer it.

slides.title: Microcontroller "ecosystems"
slides.body: Lots of sources for processor chips and development boards. But a good design depends on more than just a good set of chip specifications, or a low price. You will also need many of these:
items: Development / evaluation boards
Language support (C, C++, MicroPython, CircuitPython)
Debuggers, emulators (your Nucleo's built-in ST-LINK is one)
Real time operating system (RTOS: FreeRTOS, Zephyr)
Device drivers, APIs, examples
Data sheets and application notes
Developer community, field application engineers
slides.presenterNote: Her 17x slide 25 (her "more that just" typo corrected to "more than"; three list examples refreshed 2026-09: languages gained CircuitPython, the debugger line now points at the ST-LINK on their own board instead of at the Arduino, RTOS names FreeRTOS and Zephyr). Her notes: If you want to do a microcontroller project (89-90, etc), there is a lot of sources that want to sell you their very specific board. When you commit to buying a chip you are buying into the entire ecosystem. A good design depends on more than just the chip (and timers etc). You need the ecosystem, for example the prototyping support. A lot of boards sell evaluation boards on which you can prototype without having to solder your circuits etc. An evaluation board is (generally) a basic system built around some specific part, along with all the other stuff you need to get that part to work. Once you stick all these pieces together, and write the software, and it works, you can produce your own circuit board with all the chips on it. Don't look directly for evaluation boards — look for a part you want to have, then look for evaluation boards which have that part or a similar one. Need language support: is there a good compiler? Do they have debuggers? [Note updated 2026-09: we did use the CubeIDE debugger on Day 7x — step, breakpoint, the register view — so say 'you have done this' rather than her original 'we haven't used this in this class.'] Step-through your code. There is none for the Arduino. Or emulators, that is a piece of software that pretends to be your chip. Do you want a real operating system? In our class we are writing bare-metal C. We are running one thing at a time. This teaches you a lot. Big trend: RTOS which is the compromise between the convenience of a real OS like Linux and the precision of being able to operate in real time. An OS schedules all the different tasks that have to happen. You don't have any control over what happens when. So you are at the mercy of the OS. A RTOS is designed to keep multiple balls in the air but with precise timing that you have control over. You cannot run an RTOS on an Arduino but you can run it on a bigger microcontroller. Device drivers: Adafruit has them for all of their boards. You want that for development! Also want good data sheets and application notes. You want a good developer community and field application engineers that help you use the company's parts and help you solve your problems. You want to know the company is there for you if you need help.

slides.title: Beyond the Nucleo: other microcontroller families
items: Your STM32C031C6 is one of thousands of Arm Cortex-M microcontrollers, the most widely used family. Everything we did this term carries over: reading a reference manual, and configuring GPIO, timers, interrupts, the ADC, the UART and I2C. The register names differ from vendor to vendor, so you will still read the new part's manual.
Arm designs 32-bit processor architectures (M: microcontrollers, A: microprocessors). Other companies license and manufacture them.
STMicroelectronics (ST) alone spans the small C0 family you used up to the H7 family at the high-performance end, all on Nucleo boards ($10 to $15) with the same tools we used this term.

Other Cortex-M vendors are Microchip, NXP, Renesas, Infineon and Silicon Labs. Nordic makes the Bluetooth Low Energy radios: a Nordic radio runs the Bluefruit module in your kit, and the nRF52 and nRF54 are its current families.
slides.presenterNote: Replaces her Arduino-anchored 17x slide 23 (her ask, 2026-09-13); her Arm-licensing bullet is kept on the wall. Her note still worth telling aloud: Arm doesn't make chips — it designs the cores and licenses them to companies that fabricate; the vendors share the architecture and differ in the peripherals, which is why the manual-reading skill is the transferable one. Facts checked 2026-09: Cortex-M holds roughly two-thirds of the microcontroller market; ST announced the C0's successor line (STM32C5, Cortex-M33) in March 2026. The Bluefruit's own radio is Nordic's older nRF51822 — the chapter deliberately never names the chip, so the slide says "a Nordic radio" and stays truthful.

slides.title: Beyond the Nucleo, continued
items: Raspberry Pi's RP2350 (on the $5 Pico 2) and Espressif's ESP32 family (WiFi and Bluetooth on the chip) are newer, and they are where the low-cost end of the market has gone.
RISC-V is an open, royalty-free instruction set, and the fastest-growing one. Newer ESP32 parts use it. For a one-term project, the Arm parts still have the more mature tools.
8-bit and 16-bit processors are often adequate for small jobs: Microchip's AVR and PIC (the AVR is the classic Arduino's chip) and TI's MSP430. A 32-bit part now costs about the same.
slides.presenterNote: The rest of her 17x slide 23, updated to 2026. Her 8/16-bit note still applies: that doesn't mean smaller processors aren't useful — the keypad on your dishwasher is probably handled by an 8-bit processor; the AVR and PIC are now under the same company (Microchip). Facts checked 2026-09: Pico 2 is $5, RP2350 has dual Cortex-M33 plus dual RISC-V Hazard3 cores, boot-selectable; newer ESP32s (C3/C6) are RISC-V; RISC-V is the fastest-growing architecture.

slides.title: Suggested boards, by what the project needs
items: To stay with what you know, pick another STM32 Nucleo: G0 for general-purpose work, G4 for analog and motor control, L4 or U5 for battery life.
For WiFi or a phone app, an ESP32 development board is the cheapest way to put a project on the network.
For Bluetooth Low Energy on a coin cell, use a Nordic nRF52840 or nRF54 development board. These are the parts most commercial BLE products use.
The Raspberry Pi Pico 2 ($5) is inexpensive and very well documented, and you can program it in C or in MicroPython.
If the project needs Linux, a camera, or machine learning, it needs a small computer rather than a microcontroller: a Raspberry Pi 5, or an NVIDIA Jetson for machine-learning work ("edge computing").
Arduino is still fine for a quick prototype, and Arduino's libraries run on many of the boards above.
slides.presenterNote: New slide (her ask). One suggestion per need, so a lost student leaves with a name to type into a search box. Facts checked 2026-09: Nucleo-64 boards run $10 to $15; nRF54L15 development kits shipping since early 2025; Qualcomm's acquisition of Arduino was announced October 2025 with the UNO Q launched alongside ($44, an STM32 microcontroller beside a Linux-capable Qualcomm processor), and the UNO R4 is a Renesas Cortex-M4 — today's Arduino is Cortex-M underneath. ENGS 62 uses an Arm Cortex-A9; the A-vs-M distinction (computation vs pins, timers and peripherals) is worth one sentence aloud at the small-computer bullet.

slides.title: Where to look
items: Distributor parametric search (Digi-Key, Mouser): filter by the requirements you worked out, and by what is actually in stock.
Every vendor has an online product selector. ST's lets you filter the whole STM32 line by peripheral, memory, and package.
Adafruit and SparkFun sell breakout boards and publish drivers and tutorials for nearly every sensor you would wire to any of these.
Make: magazine publishes an annual Guide to Boards: makezine.com/comparison/boards
Before you commit, download the datasheet and the reference manual and confirm that the peripheral you need really is on that part.
slides.presenterNote: Replaces her Make:-only slide 24 with the places engineers actually search first; her resource is kept as the browse. Her note still applies to the Make: line: great hobby magazine, clever people contribute, it's the buyer's guide to the landscape of boards (the 2026 edition is Make: Volume 95, 15 boards, the UNO Q and Pi 500+ on the cover; her 2021 cover image is dropped as dated).
